title: PLATINUM
summary: PLATINUM is the vendor label for a long-running espionage activity set that public reporting has tracked since about 2009 and generally assesses as state sponsored, though the sponsor is not openly confirmed. Reported victims are concentrated in government, diplomatic, defence and related research organisations in South and Southeast Asia, with a smaller number of cases elsewhere. The distinguishing technical trait is memory-resident tradecraft: implants that patch running processes, load code without a matching file on disk, and communicate over unusual network channels including non-standard ports and protocol masquerading. Public reporting has also described abuse of Windows hotpatching, where a running process is modified in memory so the code that executes no longer matches the vendor binary on disk. For defenders this means disk-centric triage and signature scanning can return a clean result while the intrusion remains active, so reliable detection depends on memory forensics, behavioural monitoring and precise network baselining. Evidence includes anomalous parent-child process relationships, unsigned modules loaded into trusted processes, non-standard listening sockets, sparse or missing logging, and staging directories used for collection. The common misunderstanding is that a clean antivirus scan or an unchanged system file proves a host is trustworthy; in this activity set, the file on disk is often exactly the evidence the implant intends to leave untouched.

beginner.definition: PLATINUM is a name used by security companies for a long-running spying group. Public reports say it has targeted government and diplomatic organisations in Asia since around 2009. Its special skill is hiding inside the memory of a running computer. That makes it much harder to find than ordinary malware.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most tools look for bad files stored on a disk. This group often leaves no such file. A computer can look clean while an intruder is still reading its data. If your team trusts a simple virus scan, this kind of activity can stay hidden for years.
howItWorks: The attacker first gains access, often through targeted messages or a weak internet facing service.
Instead of saving a program to disk, the attacker loads code into a running process.
The running process is modified in memory so it no longer matches the file it came from.
The hidden code talks to the attacker over unusual network ports or disguised traffic.
Collected documents are stored in a staging folder and quietly sent out in small pieces.
The attacker removes or avoids logs, so investigators find few traces after the fact.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel where the reception desk keeps a list of every registered guest. A clever intruder never signs the book. He slips into a room that is already occupied, stays there, and uses the guest name on the door. A guard checking the guest list sees only familiar names and nothing unusual. That is memory-resident activity. The room key and the name are real. The person behind the door is not on any list.
takeaways: A clean file scan does not prove a computer is safe, because code can run only in memory.
Record what normal network traffic and processes look like, so unusual patterns stand out.
Collect memory data early when you suspect an intrusion, before a restart erases it.

objectives: Explain what memory-resident malware is and why disk scanning may miss it.
Describe how unusual network ports and disguised protocols appear in real traffic.
List the evidence worth collecting from a suspect host before it is rebooted.
Explain why attribution for this activity set is published with only moderate confidence.
Build a simple baseline of normal process and network behaviour for one server.
